What is the essential teaching in 'The Threefold Refuge: tisarana'?

In 'The Threefold Refuge: tisarana', the teaching opens with this observation: *"They go to many a refuge, to mountains and forests, to park and tree shrines: people threatened with danger."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text teaches, the Dhamma is *akāliko* — ever-present — and *opanayiko* — leading inward — available to be known (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner for themselves. There is no need to search elsewhere; the truth is already here.

Can you explain the teaching in the section 'A refuge supreme'?

This section teaches: *"They go to many a refuge, to mountains and forests, to park and tree shrines: people threatened with danger. That's not the secure refuge, not the supreme refuge, that's not the refuge, having gone to which, you gain release from all suffering & stress . But when, having gone to the Buddha , Dhamma , & Sangha for refuge, you see with right discernm..."* The core instruction is to turn investigation inward (*opanayiko*) toward what is already present in body, speech, and mind — not to seek the Dhamma outside or in future states. Whatever theme this section addresses, the method is the same: sustained, patient, non-grasping awareness that allows the truth to reveal itself. As Ajahn Mun taught: when the mind sees clearly, there is no longer any need to go looking.

This text mentions suffering (dukkha). Can you explain its role in practice?

In this text, dukkha appears in this context: *"That's not the secure refuge, not the supreme refuge, that's not the refuge, having gone to which, you gain release from all suffering & stress ."* Understanding suffering (dukkha) is not merely conceptual — it is meant to be verified directly. The Dhamma is *ehipassiko*: 'come and see for yourself.' Bring the quality described by dukkha into direct investigation: where is it present in your current experience? When seen clearly, each of these Pāli terms dissolves from abstract concept into living reality.
